rv.q: McDonald’s “Rose’s Turn” feels like a once-in-a-lifetime event; the sort of unequivocal theater magic that you one day tell your grandkids about.
The number, operatic in intensity and cathartic on a level few other musicals have ever achieved, simply flattens you.

It is a once-in-a-lifetime performance (yours, not hers) that anyone would be crazy to miss.
McDonald's Rose is a force of nature, a woman who refuses to be ignored or dismissed, even when her dreams have long since passed their expiration date.
In "Gypsy," McDonald augments her unparalleled Broadway legacy by summoning America’s rueful history to the stage.
In any case, no minor flaw can diminish the impact of this masterful show in such a beautifully acted production — all of it orbiting around the blazing force that is McDonald.
Any production of “Gypsy” rises or falls on its Rose, and Ms. McDonald’s lifts this staging to majestic (sorry) heights.
McDonald certain makes a good a case as anyone ever has for Rose qualifying as a tragic hero, and more power to both her and her director.
The slow striptease of this ferocious woman’s agitated mind was over, at last, and, unlike Gypsy, she showed us everything.
This is the first time on Broadway that Rose and her family have been played by Black actors, and McDonald imbues her with an extra layer of tragic defiance; her uphill climb is extra steep.
McDonald’s voice has equal parts of both, and she uses it to deliver an unforgettable star turn.

Woods is sensational, moving from heartbreaking vulnerability in “Little Lamb” to slinky, Josephine Baker-esque confidence as she embraces her Gypsy Rose Lee striptease persona. Woods also has the nerve to be hilarious, all the while going head to head with the tornado force that is McDonald.
I can’t recall a better wrong-for-the-part performance in recent memory than McDonald’s Rose.
Wolfe’s Gypsy may flicker, but McDonald glows like a furnace at its center.
But they perform the parts so enormously that they’re out of whack with the rest of the show, which has been frustratingly dialed down and never settles on a consistent tone other than dull.
Everything is indeed coming up roses for the best Gypsy and the best musical revival in years.
It’s a performance for the ages.
McDonald’s monumental performance and Wolfe’s intelligent staging make this an essential entry into the revival canon, and a production not to be missed.

Regardless, as the ads promoting this revival have suggested, this is Audra’s “Gypsy,” and one well worth catching.

McDonald’s take on Momma Rose is all her own from her very first line to her triumphant final song.
McDonald's Rose is a force of nature, delivering a performance that is both deeply personal and universally resonant.
The whole production is a rare privilege; you either got it or you ain’t — and this one’s got it.
Those theatergoers who like their musical theater on the cutting edge will find this Gypsy invigorating.
Audra is magnificent, everything’s coming up roses.
Her Rose isn’t the abominable woman we’ve seen in previous productions.
Given the meatiest role of her storied career, Audra McDonald as Rose devours the stage while creating a monstrous but sympathetic character you will not forget.
It’s an audacious production and it is also very, very dark.
McDonald seems to project her heartache from her insides directly into ours; it’s honestly difficult to witness her “Rose’s Turn” without crying.
McDonald goes all out to show us the troubled person beneath, which of itself makes this Gypsy a worthy addition.

The glitzy advertising for the Broadway revival of Gypsy (Majestic Theatre, booking through June 29, 2025) starring Audra McDonald as Mama Rose says it all: AUDRA GYPSY—two words, banner-sized, McDonald’s first name fringed with flashing bulbs, the name of the musical in dramatic red.
Audra McDonald in Gypsy makes it even more significant, something you will not forget.

McDonald doesn’t sugarcoat Rose’s ambitions for herself and her daughters June (Jordan Tyson) and Louise (Joy Woods), no matter how many people she takes advantage of, which includes her father and her boyfriend, the ulcer-ridden Herbie (Danny Burstein).
All in all Gypsy impressed me on every level, and I am sincerely excited for potential nominations when awards season rolls around.
This revival of Gypsy succeeds on the strength of Audra McDonald's powerful performance and George C. Wolfe's thoughtful exploration of its central relationships.

cn.t: Critics hail McDonald's nuanced, emotionally rich Rose as a career-defining triumph in Wolfe's traditional but deeply moving revival, though some question her vocal approach and the production's uneven pacing.

sg.ra: Center rows F-L sit just past the first-row neck-crane and just before the Row H mezz overhang bites. Sharp sightlines, clean sound, full set visible from deck to fly loft.
Panoramic top-down view with zero overhang and a steep-enough rake that no head blocks you. The better pick than center orchestra for big choreography or any show with stage-high spectacle.
Steep rake, no one in front of you, nothing cut off. You trade intimacy for a clean full-stage read at roughly a third of center-orchestra pricing.
Priced to move and close to the action, but outer seats clip the far side of the stage and you'll crane for anything upstage. Stay toward the aisle-adjacent seats or accept the compromise.

The front-mezz overhang starts clipping upstage action from Row H and fully buries anything high by Row P. You're paying mid-orchestra prices for a letterboxed view — rear mezz front rows beats this every time.
